title: Riding backward
hookLine: he rides his donkey facing the tail, and every town tells a different reason why (Nasruddin tale)

cards: A dusty road in Anatolia, a long time ago. Here comes a man on a donkey, sitting backward: face toward the tail, back toward where he's going, perfectly calm about it. People in the market stop and stare.
A child laughs. Somebody calls out: Hoca, you're on your donkey the wrong way! And Nasruddin, the teacher nobody can decide is a fool or a sage, has an answer ready.
The trouble is, every town that tells this story gives him a different answer.

teach.h: SO WE CAN SEE EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Here's one answer the tellers give. Nasruddin is riding to the school with his students walking behind him. If I face forward, he says, my back is to you, and that's rude.
If you walk in front of me, your backs are to me, and that's rude too. So I ride facing you, and we can all see each other. Problem solved.

In another telling, he just wants to see where he's been. In another, the donkey knows the way, so why watch the road? And in some, there's no reason at all: he rides backward, and the whole town argues about it.
That's a clue to who Nasruddin is. The stories belong to Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim folk tradition, and they traveled far beyond it.
Tradition places a real Nasreddin Hoca in thirteenth-century Anatolia, near the town of Akşehir, where a tomb bears his name.
But many stories gathered around him over time, and nobody can say which, if any, he really lived.
Hoca, in Turkish, means teacher: a teacher whose method is to do the ridiculous thing first and let you work out the lesson. The lesson here is about direction.
We ride through our days facing forward, eyes on the next message, the next deadline. Nasruddin turns around.

teach.h: THE ROAD BEHIND IS THE VIEW.
teach.b: From the back of a donkey, the road already traveled is the whole view: who is walking with you, what you've passed.

teach.h: NOT THE WRONG WAY. THE OTHER WAY.
teach.b: It isn't the wrong way. It's the other way, and it shows you what the front can't.

how: Nasruddin stories are told aloud across Turkey, Iran, Central Asia, the Balkans and beyond, often by parents and teachers, and each telling may give its own ending; he is often pictured riding his donkey backward.

games.q: you're Nasruddin, and your students are walking behind your donkey. which way do you sit?
o: you get off and walk with them.
games.why: in one telling he rides facing the tail: if I face forward, my back is to you, and that's rude. this way we can all see each other.

practice: Start where you are and walk your day backward, one scene at a time, toward the moment you woke up, without judging any of it.
Watch the road behind you the way Nasruddin does from his donkey: who was walking with you today, and one thing you passed without seeing. When you reach the morning, rest there.

wordCard.voice: Riding backward. Nasruddin on his donkey, facing the tail, so he can see the road behind him and the people walking with him. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: face the other way. The road behind you is part of the view. That's day thirty-eight.
